claims.text: Program.cs registers NotificationSender with AddHostedService, so every running process of the api hosts its own NotificationSender loop over the same notifications table.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-2: DonHang.Api/Program.cs:32; ASP.NET Core docs: Background tasks with hosted services

claims.text: Changes made by a transaction are not visible to other transactions until it commits, so a second copy that reads the row before the first commits 'sent' still sees 'pending'.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL docs: Transactions (tutorial 3.4) and Concurrency Control 13.2.1 Read Committed; prereq foundation.l1.transaction-intro

claims.text: Inside a transaction, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the rows it returns; other transactions that try to UPDATE, DELETE or SELECT FOR UPDATE those rows are blocked until the locking transaction commits or rolls back.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL docs: SELECT, The Locking Clause; 13.3.2 Row-Level Locks (FOR UPDATE)

claims.text: With SKIP LOCKED, selected rows that cannot be locked immediately are skipped instead of waited for; the docs name queue-like tables with multiple consumers as its use.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL docs: SELECT, The Locking Clause (NOWAIT / SKIP LOCKED)

claims.text: Row-level locks are released when the transaction ends (commit or rollback); they do not affect plain data querying: a SELECT without a locking clause reads a locked row without waiting.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL docs: 13.3.2 Row-Level Locks ('Row-level locks do not affect data querying; they block only writers and lockers to the same row')

claims.text: If the api process stops before its transaction commits, the connection is lost and PostgreSQL rolls the open transaction back, releasing its row locks and leaving the claimed rows pending.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL docs: 3.4 Transactions; prereq foundation.l1.transaction-intro (lost connection leaves none of the block's changes); NotificationQueue.cs:10-15 comment @ stage-2

claims.text: ClaimDueAsync calls db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync, then FromSql with SELECT * FROM notifications WHERE status = 'pending' AND next_attempt_at <= now ORDER BY next_attempt_at, id LIMIT batchSize FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
NotificationSender passes BatchSize = 10 and its PeriodicTimer ticks every 2 s; one round is ClaimDueAsync, SendOneAsync for each row, then CompleteAsync.
CompleteAsync calls SaveChangesAsync, which uses the transaction already begun on the DbContext instead of its own, then CommitTransactionAsync commits it.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Transactions (Controlling transactions: BeginTransaction, SaveChanges within it, Commit); NotificationQueue.cs:32-37 @ stage-2

claims.text: skip-locked.sh inserts four demo rows due 2100-01-01; sessions A-D are separate connections (sql helper); A runs in the background. With no real row waiting for a retry it prints: A demo job 1-2, B demo job 3-4, C the lock timeout ERROR plus a CONTEXT line, D all four; a trap deletes the rows.
SET lock_timeout = '1s' makes a statement that waits longer than 1 second for a lock fail with 'canceling statement due to lock timeout'.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL docs: 19.11 Client Connection Defaults, lock_timeout

claims.text: Without SKIP LOCKED, a second copy that claims while the first holds its locks waits, so it stands idle while the first sends its batch.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL docs: SELECT, The Locking Clause (a locking SELECT waits for conflicting row locks unless NOWAIT or SKIP LOCKED); skip-locked.sh session C

claims.text: Claiming a small batch keeps the transaction, and so the time its row locks are held, short; when fewer rows are due than a large batch size, one copy could lock them all while other copies find nothing to claim, and a stopped copy leaves more rows waiting.
claims.source_hint: lesson reasoning; prereq foundation.l1.transaction-intro ('keep transactions short')
